- [x] **183. A fieldset looks like a group.** No border, so the thing that makes
  a fieldset worth using is invisible. Real browsers draw a groove the legend
  breaks through, which is the interesting part: the legend sits *in* the top
  border rather than above it.
  *Depends on 181. Closes when:* a fieldset draws a border with its legend
  breaking it, in a reference render.

  **Done: corpus case `fieldset-group`, and `web-a-form` has its two groups
  back.** The interesting part is a **band**: a fieldset showing a legend gets
  no block-start border for the layout run and a band as tall as the legend
  instead, with the border recorded beside it and drawn through the middle
  afterwards. The band *replaces* that border rather than adding to it, which
  is the difference between a fieldset as tall as a browser's and one two
  pixels taller — `alo_layout::legend` is the whole rule, and it is the only
  place in the engine that knows a fieldset from any other block. The box tree
  hoists the legend to the front, because HTML draws a fieldset's **first**
  legend at the top whatever comes before it; a flex or grid fieldset is left
  alone, because lifting an item out of a layout somebody wrote is this engine
  overruling them. Two things went to the queue: 190, and the note that a
  fieldset with a `border-radius` and a legend has square corners.

- [x] **180. GIF, WebP and AVIF.** Rented. The same bound and the same refusals
  as PNG and JPEG, added to the one list the tests already walk.
  *Depends on 177. Closes when:* each decodes a frozen file and each is refused
  the same way — and an animated GIF shows its first frame rather than nothing,
  because a still picture is a better answer than a gap while item 109 is
  outstanding.
  *Scope cut on starting: AVIF went to item 269.* Its pixels are an AV1 frame,
  and no AV1 decoder was found that could be rented without `unsafe` this
  engine would have to answer for. Choosing one is a decision, so it needs an ADR, not a line in a
  manifest.

  **Done for GIF and WebP (iteration 166).** `gif` and `image-webp`, both pure
  Rust and both `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, each named in one file of
  `alo-paint`: `gif_picture.rs` and `webp_picture.rs`. JPEG moved to
  `jpeg_picture.rs` in the same change, so `picture.rs` is only the format
  sniffing and the one bound, `agreed_size`, which PNG now uses too.
  Seven frozen files in corpus case `a-picture-in-each-format`, made by Pillow
  from `a-picture`'s stripes, with the script in `origin.txt`. The cases cover
  plain, transparent and animated GIF, and lossy, lossless, extended-with-alpha
  and animated WebP. Both animated files show their first frame.
  Two size claims are bounded that the decoders would otherwise act on first:
  a GIF frame bigger than its screen, and an extended WebP's lossy bitstream
  bigger than its canvas. For the second, `image-webp` reserves memory by the
  bitstream's own header, up to 16 383 square, before comparing.
  **Mutation testing found a panic in `image-webp` 0.2.4, its newest release.**
  In an animation frame with an alpha chunk, the decoder never checks the
  lossy picture against the frame's size. After an `ALPH` chunk it also
  decodes the next chunk as that picture whatever it is named. A picture
  larger than its frame then indexes past the alpha plane and panics. Both
  variants were found and are refused in front of the decoder. Each has a
  regression test built from the frozen file, and each test panics inside the
  crate when the check is doctored out.
  Every byte of all nine frozen files is flipped through `read`. A corrupt file
  either is refused, or keeps its size, or changes size only because the
  flipped byte was the size field. A GIF screen and an animated WebP canvas
  repeat their size nowhere else, so a flip there can do that honestly.
  Still owed: AVIF (269); upstream has not been told about the panic, which
  is a person's call to make.

- [ ] **269. AVIF.** Cut from 180. An AVIF is an AV1 frame in an ISO-BMFF
  box, and the box is the easy half. The AV1 decoder is the hard half: `dav1d`
  is C, `rav1d` is a Rust translation of it that keeps a great deal of
  `unsafe`, and iteration 166 found no AV1 decoder that is both pure Rust and
  free of `unsafe` (a survey to redo in the ADR, not a settled fact). ADR 0005 says untrusted
  bytes are decoded in the least privileged process that can do it, and law 4
  says `unsafe` needs a named, reviewed boundary. Which decoder, on what
  licence, behind what boundary, is the decision.
  *Depends on 180. Needs ADR*, as its own iteration. *Closes when:* an AVIF
  decodes from a frozen file, through `picture::read` and `agreed_size` like
  the other four, and is refused the same way.

  **Decided: ADR 0021 (iteration 167).** `avif-parse` for the box and `rav1d`
  for the frame, through **`rav1d`'s own safe Rust API**, with its assembly
  off, one thread, and both named in `alo-paint`'s `avif_picture.rs`; the
  colour conversion is ours (§ 5). The survey was redone and found the same
  answer for a sharper reason: `rav1d` 1.1.0, the newest release, offers only
  dav1d's C ABI, so calling it would be `unsafe` in this repository. Its Rust
  API was merged on `main` in April 2026 (rav1d #1439, #1484) and is
  unreleased; a git pin and our own FFI are both refused (§ 2).
  ***blocked:** a `rav1d` release carrying `rust_api.rs`.* Lifted by that
  release and nothing else; ADR 0021's last section says what reopens the
  choice. Until then an AVIF is refused, and § 6 says the browser never
  claims a format it does not decode.

  `rav1d` release; VP8 and VP9 have no Rust decoder (§ 5); AAC, H.264, H.265

  from what decodes (§ 6). No code was written. Its code is cut as 289–295,

## I. Making it fast enough to use

Correctness before speed is the rule everywhere else. These are the items where
being right and being unusable are the same outcome — and **every one of them is
a claim measured on hardware or not made**.

- [ ] **113. Incremental style and layout** — recompute what changed, not the
  document. *"The largest single difference between an engine that renders a
  page and one somebody can use."*
  *Depends on 80. Closes when:* a changed attribute restyles a subtree rather
  than a document, shown by a count rather than by a stopwatch.
  ***blocked:** no measurement yet (iteration 181).* ADR 0017 § 6 decided a
  changed document is rendered again **whole**, rejected incremental style
  and layout *"now"* as *"a cache built before the behaviour it caches is
  settled"*, and wrote that this item *"waits for a measurement"*: a page
  janking on every change, measured on hardware. None has been taken, and
  replacing § 6 without one would be re-deciding an accepted ADR inside a
  code commit. Lifted by that measurement — most likely once a person uses
  the window (118) — and then it needs its own ADR on what is invalidated
  and how a test proves the incremental answer equals the whole one.

- [ ] **114. Compositing layers, and scrolling that does not repaint the world.**
  *Depends on 113.*

- [ ] **115. Off-main-thread scrolling and animation.**
  *Depends on 114.*

- [ ] **116. Hardware acceleration for paint**, once the software path is
  correct. **Needs a GPU to verify.**
  *Depends on 114.*

- [ ] **117. A performance budget somebody can hold us to**: named pages,
  measured, in CI. **Needs hardware**, and until it exists no item in this
  section may claim a speed.
  *Depends on 68.*
  *Needs design (iteration 181):* its dependency is done, but it names no
  pages, no budget and no closing condition, and this repository has no CI
  to measure in. Which pages, on what machine, measured how and failing at
  what number are decisions, written down before a number is.

## J. The browser itself

What stage 2's exit gate actually measures: a person using it.

- [ ] **118. A window, tabs, and a tab strip.** *Depends on 63, 64.*
  **Decided: ADR 0024 (iteration 181).** The window is rented — `winit`
  0.30 in `alo-window`'s `window.rs`, `softbuffer` 0.4 in its `present.rs`,
  both through safe interfaces, no `unsafe` of ours (§ 1); the event loop
  never calls a renderer, a *conductor* thread owns `Tabs`, and the window is
  **composed** by a function with a reference render from the frames it was
  last sent (§ 2); device pixels are the renderer's, and until 299 the
  window replicates pixels to the integer scale factor (§ 3); the **tab strip
  is a document we ship**, built from the browser's state as data — a title
  is a text node, never markup — and rendered in a sandboxed renderer of its
  own, so the agent reads tabs as it reads a page (§ 4); a person's pointer
  is the only coordinate that reaches a renderer, hit-tested there, and what
  a click on the strip means is claimed by its renderer and decided by the
  browser process (§ 5); a person opens a tab, and a page only by
  `target="_blank"` on a link a person activated (§ 6). No code was written.
  Cut as 296–300; 118 closes when all five have.
  *Opened by* stage 2's exit gate — *"a person uses it as their browser for
  a week"* — which nobody can begin without a window; the frozen alo pages
  in the corpus are what it shows first.

  ***Done (iteration 322).*** Which element a person's pointer is over, as
  Chrome 154 finds it:
  - **Measured**, not read from Chrome's source, with `elementFromPoint`
    over CDP on probe pages at 400 × 300 with the `dejavu` crate's sans,
    and with `Input.dispatchMouseEvent`, whose `mousedown` targets agreed
    at every point tried. A point is the pixel that starts at it: a box
    is found where it overlaps the square from (x, y) to (x + 1, y + 1)
    by some area, so a box from 10 is found at 9.05 and not 9, and a box
    at 10.25 at 9.3 and not 9.25; its far edges are exact. The box drawn
    last wins. Transforms, clips (to the padding box) and rounded
    corners are honoured. An inline box's pieces are on whole pixels,
    each edge rounded (`snap::to_whole_pixels`); other boxes are exact.
    Text is the element it is in, in the document (a `display: contents`
    span is found by its text); a point over no box inside the viewport
    is the root element.

    transforms and clips, cuts the point's pixel by each clip as it opens
    and by each area (Sutherland–Hodgman against convex shapes; a
    contour that is not convex is its bounds), and keeps the last area

- [ ] **481. ★ What alo browser is, as an application on alo OS.** *Needs ADR,
  as its own iteration.* Three things this repository cannot decide alone and
  must not guess: whether a renderer inside the rented tool's confinement can
  still apply its own user namespace and seccomp filter — and if it cannot,
  whether ADR 0010 is superseded for that platform rather than bent; how an
  address reaches a browser already running, which `alo-software`'s
  `browsing.rs` names as *the acting half* and leaves to the application; and
  the shape of the agent surface where law 2's tree meets alo OS's enumerated
  verbs, which is the whole reason a sovereign browser on a sovereign system
  is worth more than either alone. *The questions are asked of alo OS in
  writing before this is taken; `alo-os` is read-only reference and nothing
  here edits it. Depends on 131. Closes when:* the ADR answers all three with
  their answers cited, or records which are still unanswered and what this
  repository does in the meantime.

  **Asked, and answered (2026-10-12).** Their reply, so that the ADR is written
  from what they said rather than from what we inferred:

  1. **Nesting: undecided, and they refused to guess.** Their ADR 0005 settles
     that applications are Flatpaks reaching the system through XDG portals and
     is *silent* on whether one may nest its own sandbox inside that. The
     `seccomp` and `Landlock` in their tree belong to their ADRs 0013 and 0015
     and are alo OS's **own** enforcement of agent grants — a different
     mechanism pointed at a different actor — so our reading of their tree
     implied nothing. They are running our four probes under their real default
     confinement and will send the probes, the exit codes, and the kernel and
     Flatpak versions. If nesting fails they will **not** tell us to rely on
     their confinement: that would change their security story as much as
     ours, and needs an ADR on their side naming what a browser may assume.
     *A second risk neither letter named:* their image sets no `lsm=` kernel
     argument, so whether Landlock is active on alo OS at all is unrecorded.
     That is independent of nesting — if it is not enabled, ADR 0010's three
     layers cannot all apply there whatever the probes say.
  2. **The handover is decided and we had read the wrong file.** Not
     `browsing.rs`, which only answers *which* application opens an address:
     `crates/alo-software/src/opening_the_web.rs`, and the mechanism is
     **`org.freedesktop.portal.OpenURI`** — not argv, not a desktop entry with
     `%u`, not D-Bus activation. The order it judges in is load-bearing: an
     asking application holding no grant is refused **before** anything about
     the machine is read, so a refusal cannot tell it whether this machine has
     a browser or which one. That is a principle worth mirroring in our own
     refusals. Nothing outside their crate calls `opened` yet, so the contract
     is stable and its caller does not exist. The already-running case is
     **owed** — they will specify it, and we are asked not to infer it from
     Firefox.
  3. **The policy: our reasoning accepted.** `browser_configuration.rs` is
     written around a third party by its own words, and a browser with no
     telemetry empties that sentence rather than satisfying it. They accept
     that a policy file asserting a promise the engine keeps structurally is
     weaker than the structure — a policy can be edited, an absent subsystem
     cannot — and recommend to their owner that the policy be made conditional
     on the pinned browser being third-party. We are not asked to carry a
     vacuous document.
  4. **The agent surface is contracted, and the tier we want is not carried
     out.** `docs/contracts/app-adapters.md`: a browser becomes `@browser`, an
     adapter of **declared data** — an `alo_adapters::Adapter` constant whose
     verbs appear as `adapter.verb`, with `text_editor.rs` the worked example.
     Their load-time refusals (an argument that is a script, a command or free
     text; a parameter the application interprets; an action chosen by an
     argument) are our ADR 0002's *no verb takes a coordinate* arrived at
     independently. But `crates/alo-adapters/src/loading.rs:119-123` carries
     out **`Mechanism::DBus` only**; `Api` and `Accessibility` are declarable
     and refused `NotCarriedOutHere`, `Synthetic` always. Both tiers that suit
     us are uncarried — `api` for the tree, `accessibility` for item 130's
     AT-SPI floor. They asked for our input because our answer changes their
     build, and this is the one place that is true.
  5. **The source is their owner's.** `SourceName::checked` validates shape
     only, as we read it; their ADR 0005 permits Flathub *or* a repository an
     organisation runs and chooses neither. Their note to their owner favours
     public third-party review.
  6. **The identifier is ours.** No alo namespace exists to collide with;
     their list is all upstream reverse-DNS. It needs a domain the owner
     controls, and that is a decision for them and not for a loop.

  **And a correction from them that makes our position harder, recorded
  because it would be convenient to forget.** A browser *is* now on a fresh
  alo OS machine. `alo-shipping.service` carried `ConditionFirstBoot=yes`,
  which can never be satisfied on an ostree deployment, so every machine
  shipped with none of its seven applications and reported success; it is
  fixed and all seven were watched installing on a booted disk. Their roadmap
  line still said otherwise when we read it. So **this is a replacement, not a
  gap being filled**, and the plan is made on that footing.

  must not be inferred from Firefox's behaviour. A second `alo` asked to open an address while
  one is running hands it over rather than starting a rival; an address from
  another application opens in a tab. *Depends on 481, 300. Closes when:* a

  and one handed while no browser runs starts one — both asserted, and the

- [ ] **484. ★ `@browser`, as far as alo OS can carry it.** The adapter
  declaration for item 131's verbs, against
  `alo-os`'s `docs/contracts/app-adapters.md` — declared data, an
  `alo_adapters::Adapter` constant, `Mechanism::DBus` because that is the one
  tier their loader carries out and a declaration that answers
  `NotCarriedOutHere` cannot be gated at all. *Depends on 131, 480, 481.*

  **What they confirmed is declarable (2026-10-12), from their loader rather than
  their prose:**
  - `read()` — no arguments, effect `read`, `reaches: OnlyItsApplication`.
  - `activate(name)` — the element as `Kind::Name { longest }`, **and the
    D-Bus method named as a literal**. Their loader refuses *an action chosen
    by an argument*, so one verb per action; a dispatching method earns
    `NotLoaded::ChoosesWhatRuns`, whose words would blame our argument for a
    fault in our method.
  - `fill(field, text)` — **only with `Kind::Name`, and only for values with no
    slash.** `Kind::Text` is refused outright (`NotLoaded::TakesCode`): *"text
    a model writes is not an argument."* `Name` additionally refuses empty, a
    control character, `.`, `..`, over `longest`, and `/` or `\`. So a name, an
    amount, an email address or a search phrase can be filled; **a date
    written `12/10/2026` cannot**, and would be refused with `NotOneName` —
    filename words, in a browser, to a person filling in a date.
  - **Every verb needs `by_hand`** — how a person does the same thing
    themselves — or `NoByHand`. **Every `Word` must appear in the adapter's
    `words` list** or `WordNotDeclared`. Neither was in our letter.

  **What cannot be declared at all, and is theirs to fix:**
  - `open(address)`. `Takes` is a closed list of five — `Path`, `Application`,
    `Name`, `Count`, `Choice` — and none of them is a web address. `Path`
    demands a grant over a machine path; `Name` refuses the slashes every URL
    contains. They *have* `alo_software::WebAddress` and it is not an argument
    kind. Their own comment settles the order: adding to `Takes` belongs in
    their ADR 0001 and their `agent-verbs.md` before it belongs in code. **Do
    not declare `open` as a `Name`** — it would load and then refuse every real
    address at validation, which is the worst of both.
  - Model-written text that may legitimately contain a slash. No kind for it.
  - **A grant narrower than an application** — and this is the large one.
    `Reaches` offers only `Over(paths)` and `OnlyItsApplication`. Granting
    `@text_editor` grants a text editor; granting `@browser` would grant every
    page a person can reach — their mail, their bank, their employer — as one
    approval over one application. Their grant model has no vocabulary for a
    *site*, and they have put that to their owner as ADR 0001's natural
    extension to the web. **This is the reason this item cannot simply be
    built small and shipped**, and it is not a fault in item 131's shape:
    their letter says the shape is right and their models are short of it.

  ***Answered, and this item shrank (2026-10-12).*** Two of their answers
  change it. `Takes` and `Reaches` are **not scheduled** — no task in their
  repository carries a web-address argument kind or a narrower `Reaches` — so
  this adapter is thin **by decision rather than by waiting**: `read()` and
  `activate(name)`, and not `open(address)`. And they asked us **not** to speak
  D-Bus natively: nothing of theirs carries out an adapter verb at all
  (`Delivers`, `Driving` and the session bus are reached only from tests), so
  D-Bus would buy no verifiability and a shape adopted for one system would be
  carried for years. Their words: *build the right interface for every system;
  we will write the wrapper, and that is our debt rather than your delay.* So
  item 496 is the real work and this is a wrapper they may write themselves.
  *Depends on 496.*

  *Closes when:* the declarable subset above loads on a real alo OS machine,
  each verb's refusals asserted, and the three gaps recorded as theirs.

- [x] **496. ★ The interface an agent outside this browser speaks.** *Needs
  ADR, as its own iteration.* Item 131 built the capability — a page nobody
  wrote for us read as a tree and driven by name — and **nothing outside the
  process can reach it.** `alo-agent`'s `Verb`, `Outcome`, `Target` and
  `Refusal` cross into the renderer (`alo-renderer/src/message.rs:85`), and no
  binary accepts a verb: `grep Verb crates/alo-window/src` is empty. So the
  one thing this project justifies itself by has no consumer.

  ***The ADR is written: ADR 0055 (2026-10-12), and this is next by the owner's
  choice.*** It is numbered 0055 and not 0053 because the loop committed its
  own 0053 first and 0054 was already in flight. So this item is **not** a
  decision iteration any more — the decision is made and this is its code.
  ADR 0055 settles: a Unix domain socket the browser process holds and
  **never a port**, because a page's own script can reach `localhost` and a
  port would let any page read every tab and type into every field with no
  grant consulted; the browser process answering and never a renderer, so
  ADR 0005 survives; **a refusal crossing as a kind with its own fields**, so
  our English never becomes a caller's dependency; **a tab named by its
  address** rather than numbered, because an index is the coordinate ADR 0002
  refuses; the grant checked **before any tab is looked at**, so a refusal
  cannot reveal what a person has open; and the record written by the browser
  process, because a renderer that could write it could lie. macOS and Linux
  use `std::os::unix::net`; **Windows is undecided** in that ADR and is not
  this item's problem.

  **The ADR decides what a contract decides, because outsiders build against
  it and contracts outlive code** — alo OS's warning, earned on their own
  adapter format. It must settle: how an agent outside the process reaches a
  running browser; how a verb, a target and a refusal are encoded; how a tab
  is named when several are open; what the record of an action is and who
  writes it; and what a refusal says, since every refusal in `verb.rs` —
  `NotFound`, `Ambiguous`, `NotOperable`, `Disabled`, `ReadOnly`, `NotADate`,
  `TooLong` and the rest — has to survive the crossing without becoming a
  string.

  **It is ours and the same everywhere.** macOS, Windows and Linux alike
  (`ROADMAP.md`, *Where it runs*), and **not D-Bus**: ADR 0052's addendum
  records why, and alo OS asked for this shape rather than theirs.

  *Depends on 131. Closes when:* an agent in a **separate process** reads a
  frozen real page as a tree, completes a task on it by name, and the record
  says what was read and what changed — asserted in a test, with every refusal
  reachable by name and none of them a string a caller has to parse.

  ***Done (iteration 304).*** `alo-window` holds the socket (`agents.rs`)
  at a private place (`socket_place.rs`), and the conductor answers on the
  thread that holds the tabs (`serving.rs`). `protocol.rs` is the one file
  that names `serde_json`, rented, and `asking.rs` is what a line means.
  The record is `agent_record.rs`, handed back by `Conductor::records`. The
  `alo` binary opens the socket and says where it is, and `alo-ask` is the
  smallest caller. The contract is `docs/contracts/agent-socket.md`, version
  1, additive only. In `an_agent_outside_the_browser.rs`, `alo-ask`, a
  separate process, does the closing condition on the frozen `web-a-form`
  over the real renderer program: it lists the tabs, reads the form, fills

- [ ] **549. ★ A window nobody is watching is not drawn.** `alo` always opens
  a window and asks it to redraw; its only flags are `--agent-site`, `--fonts`
  and `--frozen-fonts`. So every task an agent drives pays for painting a
  picture nobody looks at.

  **Nothing about the agent changes, and that is the point.** The tree an
  agent reads is made from the layout tree — `Snapshot::of(&tree)` in
  `alo-renderer/src/renderer.rs` — and never from pixels, so a page laid out
  but not painted answers every verb identically. Screenshot-driven tools have
  a whole class of bug here, working with a window and failing without one;
  this cannot, because it never looked at a picture.

  **What it is really for is where there is no screen.** A server, a scheduled
  job, a machine in a cupboard — which is where an agent actually runs. It
  also ends this repository's dependence on somebody's screen being unlocked,
  which has stopped item 296 twice.

  rendered for the agent rather than for a person. The first half of that does
  not work — a modern page is a program, and the frozen `alo-workplace` entry

  right and nobody had written it down.*

  against each other in one test; nothing calls `winit` on that path; and a
  windowed run still paints, so the two modes are a choice rather than a
  replacement.

- [x] **627. ★ What a person looks at, on the product path.** *ADR 0058 § 2

  product path that is not a smaller version of something already built.

  rather than argued. *Depends on 619. Closes when:* the ADR is accepted, a
  page loaded through Chrome is visible in a run a person can watch, and what
  they see is asserted — frames arriving, or a window placed — in numbers

  argued, and the measurements are in the ADR: a frame costs 34 ms to encode
  and 81 KiB on the wire at 1200×800 scale 2 — a ceiling of 29.7 frames a

  and the lossy format came out *larger* than the lossless one, because an
  interface is flat colour and text. A screencast is cheaper than that only
  because it shrinks the picture: asked for 1000×700 it sent 756×469. And a

  product path for ever. Against that, Chrome in `--app` mode has no tab

  the position is legal, and `Overlay.highlightNode` draws the mark on the

  windows, one of ours tracking the other, which is the riskiest thing on the
  product path. **That is what this item now closes on**, and the ADR says it
  may send us back. Screencast is refused as the way a person looks at a

- [x] **639. What a page's script said while a verb ran, through Chrome.**
  *Cut from 630; ADR 0055, `docs/contracts/agent-socket.md`.* An answer's

  against Chrome 155.0.8059.86 from a Node CDP probe in the scratchpad:
  with `Runtime.enable` sent, a page's console calls and uncaught throws
  are told of through the tab's session (a same-process frame's too) as
  `Runtime.consoleAPICalled` and `Runtime.exceptionThrown`, each before a
  later `Runtime` command's answer; `Runtime.enable` first tells again of
  everything said before, and `Runtime.discardConsoleEntries`, taken while
  the domain is off, forgets it; an accessor on an error's `stack` is not
  called in describing it; a promise rejected and unhandled is told of a
  task later. **And a page decides how long a message is**: a 20-million

  `chrome_protocol::skipped` names it by its `id` or `method`, and an
  answer too long is `Failed::TooLong` to whoever asked, at once. A tab

  places and Chrome's words, bounded (64 values, 32 places, 1024
  characters of any text the page chose) and refusing anything else as a
  kind; `chrome_said.rs` says them in the engine's words — `the click:` /
  `the text:`, `uncaught:` and the thrown value by the engine's rules,
  ` (at …; called from …)`, at most 256 lines and the engine's count of
  the rest. **Where they differ**: Chrome places a script by its address
  and the line in the page, the engine by `script 1` and the line in the
  script; a console call is said as `console.log:` and its values through
  Chrome, where the engine, which has no console, says `uncaught:
  ReferenceError: 'console' is not defined`; an error is said by the first
  line of Chrome's description, made when it was constructed; an
  unhandled rejection is heard only if Chrome told of it before the verb's

  wire's. Cut: 652 (frames and workers in targets of their own) and 653
  (messages held by count, not size).

  a build of that crate alone carries the feature too. **Tests:**
  `alo-paint`'s `a_letter_at_a_weight.rs` builds a font with 33

- [x] **644. A renderer left stopped, and the one test that stops one.**
  *Numbered 643 by mistake when it was written, and renumbered within the
  minute: 643 was already "a placed window that stays where a person sees
  it", cut from 627. Identity is allocated once and never reused (ADR
  0003), and that holds for queue numbers.*
  `a_renderer_that_never_answers_leaves_the_window_answering_with_its_last_frame`
  failed the supervisor's gate on 2026-10-24 at 21:10 as **`FAIL + LEAK` in
  5.007 s**, stopping the loop. It has not been reproduced since: five runs of
  it alone under load, four of the whole 292-test package, and a full gate of
  5193 tests all passed, the gate in 555 s against the failing run's 1585 s —
  so the machine was about three times slower then than now, and whatever that
  was is not understood either. What is known, and is written here rather than
  acted on because **none of it has been made to fail on purpose**:
  - It is the only test that sends a renderer `kill -STOP` (line 187), and it
    never sends `-CONT` or `-KILL`. A stopped process cannot run a handler.
  - A renderer inherits the test binary's stderr (`host.rs`, `.stderr(
    Stdio::inherit())`, and the comment there says why), so **any renderer
    that outlives the test holds the pipe open and nextest reports `LEAK`.**
  - Every path that drops a renderer from the table goes through
    `Renderers::stop`, which is `kill()` — SIGKILL, which a stopped process
    does take — and then `wait()`. So the obvious defect is not there.
  - The run captured **no panic text**, which is what a test that is killed
    rather than one that fails an assertion looks like.
  - `sandbox::confined` means the process `stop()` kills may not be the
    process the test stopped. That is the first thing to check and it is a
    guess.
  *Depends on nothing. Closes when:* the failure is reproduced on purpose —
  by slowing the machine, by holding the renderer, or by stopping the
  grandchild rather than the child — and then either fixed with a test that
  fails without the fix, or shown to be a property of nextest's leak
  detection and the test changed to resume what it stopped. **It may close as
  "the test must undo its own `-STOP`", which is one line and would have been
  a guess today.**
  ***Done (iteration 381).*** **Reproduced on purpose, and it was not the
  stop.** With 96 `yes` processes on this machine's eight cores, the test
  failed three runs in three as **`FAIL + LEAK` in 5.03–5.23 s**, the
  gate's signature, panicking at its first `News::Painted`: *"the renderer
  for file:(null #2) is gone: it said nothing for 4s, so it was stopped"*.
  The test's `PATIENCE` of four seconds bounded the page's **first load and
  paint** as well as the silence after `-STOP`, and that paint takes 0.4 s
  idle, 1.2 s at 24 busy processes, 5.5–6.1 s at 96 and 12 s at 192 — so
  under a loaded gate the renderer was given up on before it was ever
  stopped. The leak is the renderers a panicking test leaves alive, which
  exit on reading the end of their pipe more than nextest's 100 ms after
  the test does. The gate's log keeps only its last twenty lines (`tail -n
  20`), so "no panic text" was the log, not a killed test. **The fix:** the
  test gives a renderer `LONGEST_SILENCE`, `alo`'s own ten seconds — a test
  may not be stricter than the browser it tests — and passes three in three
  at 96 and two in two at 192. The same four seconds was in three sibling
  tests: `the_strip_in_the_window` failed two in two at 192 with it (its
  strip given up on), and with `alo`'s bound passes there; it and
  `a_window_on_a_screen_at_its_scale`, which stop nothing, now use the
  default, and `a_strip_that_never_answers`, which stops the strip's, uses
  `LONGEST_SILENCE` too. **Those two were not made to fail** at either load;
  they changed because the defect is the same, not because it was seen.
  **The stopped renderer was a real hazard, but not the gate's:** a test
  that fails after its `-STOP`, run directly rather than under nextest,
  leaves its renderer orphaned and stopped for good (`TN`, parent 1), seen
  twice, holding the output pipe open so whatever reads it waits too.
  Under nextest each test has a process group of its own, and the system
  continues an orphaned group's stopped members, so the gate could not show
  it. Both tests that stop a renderer now hold it in a `Stopped` guard that
  kills it, if it is still one of the test's renderers, when the test ends:
  with a failure injected after the stop, nothing was left, twice. Each
  test now takes ten seconds more than it did.

- [x] **647. The second race in the agent's navigation cause.** The fix on
  2026-10-24 at 18:10 closed one race in
  `an_agents_activate_that_navigates_names_the_action_as_its_cause` and that
  test has since stopped the loop twice more — 23:46 and 06:25 — failing in
  about one second where it normally takes 1.75. It has not been reproduced
  by hand: six runs of the whole 296-test package under load, and a full
  untruncated workspace run of 5236, all green. **It fails only in the gate's
  own runs**, and why that is, is not understood.
  *The hypothesis, from reading rather than from evidence:* `Causes::of_page`
  now asks whether the document a verb was carried out in is still the one
  the tab holds, and answers `Cause::Agent` when it is. If Chrome pauses the
  **new** page's stylesheet before this process has applied that page's
  `Page.frameNavigated`, the tab still holds the old document, the action is
  still "here", and the stylesheet is pinned on the agent in the page that
  never asked for it — the same symptom as before, one step earlier.
  Against the hypothesis: Chrome commits a document before parsing it, and
  CDP messages arrive in order, so the commit *should* already have been
  read. Something about that is wrong and it has not been found.
  *What would settle it:* the panic text, which no gate ever printed until
  `gate.sh` was fixed this morning — so **the next occurrence will say what
  cause it actually got**, and the first thing to read is whether the
  document in it is the old page or the new one.
  *What the principled fix probably needs:* the request's own document
  identity from Chrome rather than this process's idea of the current page.
  `Fetch.requestPaused` carries a frame but no loader, so that identity may
  have to come from `Network.requestWillBeSent`'s `loaderId` — which is a
  design change, not a patch, and is why nothing was changed today.
  *Depends on nothing. Closes when:* the failure is reproduced on purpose,
  the cause it produces is read rather than guessed, and the fix carries a
  test that fails without it.
  ***Read at last (2026-10-25 16:28), and the hypothesis was right.*** The
  gate printed it, the first failure since `gate.sh` was taught to say why:

      the second sheet is not its page's: GET http://localhost:54740/next.css
      (style), caused by action#0, in document#0

  **`document#0` is the old page.** So Chrome asks for the new page's
  stylesheet before this process has applied that page's
  `Page.frameNavigated` — Chrome's preload scanner reads the response bytes
  before the document commits — and the tab still holds the old document, so
  the action is still "here" and the sheet is pinned on the agent in a page
  that never asked for it.
  ***And the cheap fix is refused by a decision already made.*** Attributing
  a sub-resource to the *arriving* document while a navigation is under way
  would fix this and break
  `what_the_old_page_asks_for_before_the_new_one_commits_is_the_old_pages`,
  which says in so many words that a beacon the old page sends in that window
  is the old page's. Both are true, so **the cause cannot be decided from
  which page is current**: it needs the request's own document, which

  `Runtime` is turned on only in the tab's own session, so a frame from
  another site, a dedicated or shared worker and a service worker — each a
  target of its own (`chrome_hold`) — say nothing an answer hears. A
  same-process frame's console is heard (measured). The engine runs no
  frames or workers' script that an agent's verb reaches today, so there
  is no engine answer to match yet. *Depends on 639. Closes when:* a frame
  from another site and a dedicated worker that write to their consoles
  and throw while a verb runs are heard through Chrome, with the same
  forgetting before and the same barrier after in each target, asserted
  in a test — or this item closes saying which Chrome does not tell of.
  ***Done (iteration 393).*** Measured against Chrome 155.0.8059.86,
  headless, from a Node CDP probe over a pipe in the scratchpad
  (`m652/probe2.mjs`, `probe3.mjs`): a frame from another site and a
  dedicated worker each answer `Runtime.discardConsoleEntries`,
  `Runtime.enable` and `Runtime.disable` in their own sessions; told to
  tell without forgetting first, each tells again of everything it said
  since it started (about 80 lines over two seconds, where forgetting left
  only the 40 said in the one-second click); and held before it runs,
  each answers `Runtime.enable` in 12 to 21 ms. **Two things Chrome does
  not tell of while a verb holds the page's own thread:** a dedicated
  worker of the page's uncaught throw (Chrome hands it to the page's thread
  first, as the `Worker`'s `error` event, and tells of it only once that
  thread is free — 0 throws told in a held second against 10 for the
  frame), and a worker the page starts in that task, which does not start
  until the thread is free; and a frame's `postMessage` sent from a task
  waiting on a synchronous request was not delivered before it ended.
  `chrome_hold.rs`: `Kind::is_heard` (a frame and a dedicated worker) and
  `Holding::heard`. `chrome_tab.rs`: `hear` forgets and then tells in the
  tab's session and in each such target, `heard` stops each as a barrier
  of its own, a target held while a verb is heard is told to tell before
  it is let go, and `ask_held` answers `false` rather than failing for a
  target that ended while asked — refused or never answered; a reply is no
  longer dropped for coming through a session the tab does not hold, since
  its asker may be waiting for it. Asserted in
  `what_a_frame_and_a_worker_said_through_chrome.rs`, real headless
  Chrome: a page at `127.0.0.1` holds a frame from `localhost` and a worker,
  the frame a worker of its own and a fresh worker every quarter second,
  each saying when; two one-second clicks each hear the frame's console and
  throws, its worker's console and throws, the page's worker's console and
  a worker started during the click — every line placed by its own script
  and every moment said between the verb's start and its answer.
  Mutations, restored from copies and checked with `cmp`: no forgetting in
  the targets — fails (a moment before the verb); never telling them —
  fails; a target held mid-verb not told — fails (no worker started during
  the click heard). **Not caught:** leaving the targets' `Runtime` on after
  the verb, since what they say then is dropped by the tab either way; the
  barrier is argued from Chrome's answering order, measured for the page in
  639, not asserted for a frame. Shared and service workers are cut to 654.

- [x] **654. What a shared or service worker says while a verb runs,
  through Chrome.** *Cut from 652 (iteration 393); ADR 0055.* Neither is
  heard: a shared worker's script is every connected page's, not the
  tab's, and is held on Chrome's own session (item 637); a service
  worker's runs for every page it controls and answers nothing before it
  runs (`chrome_hold`). Whether either's lines belong in one tab's
  `issues` at all is undecided, and nothing has been measured of what
  Chrome tells of them. *Depends on 652. Closes when:* each, writing to
  its console and throwing while a verb on the page runs, is measured
  through its own session, and is either heard, with a test, or this item
  closes saying why its lines are not one verb's.
  ***Done (iteration 394), heard.*** Measured against Chrome
  155.0.8059.86, headless, from Node CDP probes over a pipe in the
  scratchpad (`m654/probe.mjs`, `probe2.mjs`) holding every target as the
  tab does: a shared worker (attached through Chrome's own session) and a
  service worker (through the tab's) each answer
  `Runtime.discardConsoleEntries`, `Runtime.enable` and `Runtime.disable`
  in their own sessions within a millisecond while they run; with
  forgetting, a one-second hold of the page's thread heard 15 lines and 5
  throws from each, every one said inside it; without, each told again of
  20 lines and 6 throws said before. **Unlike a dedicated worker's, what
  each throws is told of while the page's thread is held.** The tab's own
  session hears neither. Held, a shared worker started in the held task
  answers `Runtime.enable` once the page's thread is free, before it runs;
  a service worker answers only once it runs, as with `Network.enable`.
  **Why their lines are the verb's:** a shared worker's script is every
  page's that connects to it and a service worker's every page's it
  controls, and in this browser those are all one tab's — a `Tab` borrows
  its Chrome whole and closes any tab its page opens before it loads — so
  they are the page's script as a dedicated worker's is.
  `chrome_hold.rs`: `Kind::is_heard` is every kind held. `chrome_tab.rs`:
  one started while a verb is heard is told to tell as it is held, and a
  service worker is let go without waiting on that answer. Asserted in
  `what_a_shared_and_a_service_worker_said_through_chrome.rs`, real
  headless Chrome: a page at `127.0.0.1` starts a shared worker and a
  service worker that takes it over, each saying when every 50 ms and
  throwing every fourth; two one-second clicks each hear both workers'
  console lines and throws, every moment between the verb's start and its
  answer, and the first hears a second service worker it registers start.
  Passed four runs. Mutations, restored from copies and checked with
  `cmp`: the old `is_heard` — fails (nothing heard); the service worker
  held for its answer — fails (the verb waits 30 s on it); no forgetting
  in the targets — fails (a line from before the verb). **Found, cut to
  655:** a service worker stopped (`ServiceWorker.stopAllWorkers`) keeps
  its target, answers nothing until it starts again, and starts again
  waiting on the browser in that same target, with no new attach — so it
  is never let go. Chrome did not stop one held by the tab, idle forty
  seconds, on its own.

- [x] **653. Chrome's messages are held by count, not by size.** *Found
  building 639 (iteration 391).* `chrome.rs` holds at most 256 messages
  read off the pipe until they are taken (`HELD_MESSAGES`), each at most
  16 MiB, so a page whose script writes long lines to its console while a
  verb runs could have the browser process hold some 4 GiB while the tab
  reads them. Nothing bounds that in bytes. *Depends on nothing. Closes
  when:* what is held waiting is bounded in bytes as well as in messages,
  with a test that a far side sending messages near the bound faster than
  they are taken is held to that bound.
  ***Done (iteration 398).*** `chrome_held.rs`, a hold of its own between
  the thread reading Chrome's pipe and whoever takes from it, replaces the
  standard library's `sync_channel`: a message is held only while fewer
  than `HELD_MESSAGES` (256) are and its bytes with everything held come
  to no more than `chrome.rs`'s `HELD_BYTES`, two of the longest message
  (32 MiB); past either the reader waits, and Chrome's writing with it. A
  message is always held when nothing else is, so one past a bound set
  below the longest message slows the pipe rather than stopping it. What
  a message weighs is what it holds once read — its texts, the `result`
  or `params` JSON written again, and its own size — counted by
  `chrome.rs`'s `weight`. A taker gone answers a waiting reader at once
  and lets go of what was held; a reader gone ends the taker once
  everything told is taken. `Chrome::held_bytes` says what is held.
  Tests: seven unit tests in `chrome_held.rs` (order and weight, the byte
  bound and exactly at it, the count bound, a message heavier than the
  bound held alone, the end after the reader goes, a waiting reader
  answered when the taker goes, a faster teller held to the bound), and in
  `chrome_over_a_pipe.rs` a far side standing where Chrome would that
  writes the same 4 MiB event as fast as the pipe takes it: what is held
  is watched until it settles, never past 32 MiB and within two messages
  of it; three messages taken are each the event, whole and in order; and
  what is held after is still within the bound. Mutation, restored from a
  copy and checked with `cmp`: the byte bound ignored — fails (33,555,128
  held, past 33,554,432). **Not caught:** the one-message rule removed
  hangs a unit test rather than failing it. Not bounded: the one message
  the reader has in hand while it waits, and the one Chrome is part-way
  through writing, each at most 16 MiB.

- [x] **655. A service worker that stops and starts again is never let
  go.** *Found building 654 (iteration 394); ADR 0060 § 2.* Measured
  against Chrome 155 from a Node CDP probe: a service worker the tab holds,
  stopped through `ServiceWorker.stopAllWorkers`, keeps its target and
  session, answers nothing sent to it while stopped, and when a request of
  the page starts it again it waits on the browser (`starting`) in that
  same target — no `Target.attachedToTarget` is told of, so `chrome_tab.rs`
  never asks it to pause or lets it go. The page's request through it then
  waits for ever, and a verb that asks a stopped one to tell of its script
  (item 654) waits until Chrome's patience runs out. Chrome did not stop a
  held, idle one on its own in forty seconds, past the thirty after which
  it stops one nobody holds; what else stops one — memory, a crash, an
  update of its script — is not measured. *Depends on 654. Closes when:*
  what stops a held service worker is measured, and one that stops and
  starts again is paused and let go as at its first start (from
  `ServiceWorker.workerVersionUpdated` or what Chrome tells of instead), a
  verb meanwhile neither waits on it nor hears what it said before, with a
  test that stops one between two verbs — or this item closes saying what
  of that Chrome does not allow.
  ***Done (iteration 397).*** Measured against Chrome 155.0.8059.86,
  headless, from Node CDP probes over a pipe in the scratchpad
  (`m655/probe.mjs`, `probe2.mjs`) holding every target as the tab does.
  **What stops a held one:** `ServiceWorker.stopWorker`,
  `ServiceWorker.stopAllWorkers` (once `ServiceWorker.enable` is sent) and
  a `Target.closeTarget` of its own target each stop it alike: it keeps
  its target and session, Chrome tells that session
  `Inspector.targetCrashed`, and a command sent then is answered only once
  it starts again. `Target.crash` is not a method a service worker's
  session knows; an update of its script makes a new version in a **new**
  target, attached and held as any other, and the old one's ends
  (`Target.detachedFromTarget`) — already handled. Memory pressure and a
  crash of its process were not measured. **Starting again:** the page's
  next request through it starts it in the same session, told of as
  `Inspector.targetReloadedAfterCrash` with no new attach, its script not
  run and the page's request waiting until `Runtime.runIfWaitingForDebugger`
  is sent there; it then answers `Fetch.enable`, `Target.setAutoAttach`,
  `Network.enable` and `Runtime`'s forget, enable and disable within a
  millisecond, **before it runs** — where at its first start it answers
  only once it runs — and its requests were still paused and its
  WebSocket still told of though nothing was asked again.
  `chrome_hold.rs`: `Holding` keeps each target's id and whether it has
  stopped — `stopped`, `is_stopped`, `hold_again`, `targets` — and `heard`
  passes over a stopped one. `chrome_tab.rs`: `Inspector.targetCrashed`
  through a held service worker's session marks it stopped and stops
  hearing it; `ask_held` answers `false` for one that stopped while asked;
  `Inspector.targetReloadedAfterCrash` asks it everything its first hold
  asked (`ask_to_hold`, now shared with `attached`), waiting on every
  answer, forgetting and telling if a verb is heard and told to stop
  telling if none is, and lets it go once answered; and
  `Tab::stop_service_workers_for_tests` closes each held service worker's
  target, for the test. Asserted in
  `a_service_worker_stopped_and_started_again_through_chrome.rs`, real
  headless Chrome, at a patience of 15 s: a page at `127.0.0.1` whose
  service worker takes it over, ticks every 50 ms and answers `/x` by
  fetching `/from-sw`; a click hears it; stopped, a click is answered in
  under 5 s and hears nothing of it; the page's fetch then starts it again
  and its `/from-sw?again` is paused in its own target, let go and
  received by the server; and the next click hears it again, every line
  said while that click ran. Passed five runs alone and three under 96
  busy processes. Mutations, restored from copies and checked with `cmp`:
  the stop not read — fails (the click waits out Chrome's patience); the
  start not read — fails (`/from-sw?again` never received). **Not
  caught:** a worker started again not told to forget, or not told to
  stop telling between verbs, since what it says then is dropped either
  way; and `ask_held`'s answer for one that stops while asked, since the
  stop is read before the verb asks it in the test.

- [x] **656. A frame's next document's fetch, pinned on the document
  before it.** *Found in iteration 394's first gate run; ADR 0012, item

  frame's `Page.frameNavigated` for the new document — the shape of item
  647's hypothesis, on a frame's own target rather than the tab's, and
  with no verb running. Not reproduced: the test passed 20 runs alone and
  30 under 96 busy processes. The change of iteration 394 cannot reach it
  — what it touched runs only while a verb is heard, and the test runs
  none. *What would settle it:* the same as 647's — the request's own
  loader from Chrome (`Network.requestWillBeSent`'s `loaderId`, or a
  paused request's frame checked against the commit it waits behind)
  rather than this process's idea of the frame's current document.
  *Depends on 636. Closes when:* the failure is reproduced on purpose, the
  order Chrome told things in is read rather than guessed, and the fix
  carries a test that fails without it — or it closes with 647 if one
  fix is the other's.
  ***Done with 647 (iteration 400), one fix being the other's.*** A
  frame's window is the tab's own frame's in `Causes::window`, its first
  hop's `networkId` kept and what it asks for owed in `chrome_owed.rs`,
  and the renderer asked through the session its commit came by — the
  frame's own target for one from another site. **Reproduced on purpose**
  by the same relay, holding the other-site frame's commit of its second
  page until that page's `fetch` is paused:
  `a_frames_new_documents_fetch_chrome_pauses_before_the_document_is_its_own`
  failed without the fix exactly as iteration 394's gate did (`caused by

- [x] **657. An old page's request paused after the new page's commit.**
  *Found measuring 647 (iteration 400); ADR 0012, ADR 0060's amendment of
  25 October.* The same race as 647 the other way round: Chrome 155,
  under 96 busy processes, told of a new page's commit and *then* paused
  requests the old page made as it was left — a `sendBeacon` from
  `pagehide` in 55 of 60 runs. 647 decides only
  the window between a first hop and its commit, so these are written as
  the **new** page's. A request with a `networkId` could be decided the
  same way, by its loader, if a line were owed for every request paused
  before its `requestWillBeSent` and not only in the window — which owes
  most of a page's lines for a moment and needs its own bound. A beacon,
  a `keepalive` fetch and a picture asked for in `pagehide` carry no
  `networkId` at all and are never told of, so nothing Chrome says names
  their document: what this process knows is only that the old page was
  being left, and whether that is enough is the question.
  *Depends on 647. Closes when:* a request the old page made, paused
  after the new page's commit is read, is recorded as the old page's —
  or the record says, by name, that it cannot tell — with a test that
  fails without it.
  ***Done (iteration 401).*** **It was one question, not two.** Measured
  against Chrome 155.0.8059.86 with a CDP probe: all 391 requests a page
  made in `pagehide`, `unload` and `visibilitychange` as a link was
  followed — beacons, `keepalive` fetches, plain fetches, pictures —
  were paused with **no `networkId`**, under 96 busy processes, and none
  was ever told of by `requestWillBeSent`; 312 were paused after the new
  page's commit was read, and with the new page on another site that was
  every one, on a quiet machine too (30 of 30). Every request of a living
  page had a `networkId`: 240 of the new page's, its own beacon and
  `keepalive` fetch among them, and 31 kinds on a page asking for
  everything it can, headless and shown. So a frame remembers the
  document it **left** from its commit until its next navigation's first
  hop, and a request paused through a frame's session with no
  `networkId` is that document's (`Causes::of_unnamed`); before the
  commit it is the document held, as before. Nothing is owed or waited
  for. ADR 0060's second amendment decides it: an absent id, like a
  loader, chooses between two documents this process minted. The relay of
  `a_page_chrome_tells_of_after_what_it_asks_for.rs` now also holds a
  paused request back behind a commit; its new test holds a self-sent
  page's beacon behind the new page's commit and asserts the beacon and
  the `keepalive` fetch are the page left's. Mutations: the tab using
  `of_frame` — the test fails, *pinned on the page arrived*; the first
  hop not clearing the page left — the unit test fails. Not decided: a
  shared or service worker's request with no id stays the page's (none
  measured), and a living page's request with none would be the page
  left's until the next navigation (none seen).

- [x] **658. An option of a closed list, through a shown Chrome.** *Cut
  from 648 (iteration 402); ADR 0064 § 6.* A closed `<select>`'s option
  has no box in Chrome, and on macOS the only key that changes a closed
  list headless is type-ahead, which chooses each option it passes and
  tells the page of each — a list that sends its page wherever it says
  would be followed to the first. So ADR 0064 refuses it by name. A person
  opens the list's menu, which on macOS Chrome draws as a menu of the
  system's own, and whether the `Input` domain reaches that menu, whether
  it holds the page while open, and whether a key or a click in it then
  chooses with one `change`, is not measured: the screen was locked.
  *Depends on 660 (it was 648's; iteration 403 cut 648). Closes when:*
  that is measured with the screen in use,
  and either a closed list's option is chosen through a shown Chrome with
  the page hearing one `input` and one `change` for the option asked, in
  a test, or ADR 0064 says why it stays refused.
  ***Decided, not built (iteration 433): ADR 0071.*** Measured with the
  screen in use against Chrome 156.0.8078.73: CDP's click opens macOS's
  menu (a layer-101 window of Chrome's process) and the page goes on;
  CDP's keys reach only the page; keys posted to Chrome's process with
  `CGEventPostToPid` — from `osascript` too — move the menu's highlight
  over the options it can highlight and Return chooses, the page hearing
  one `input` and one `change`; another application brought in front
  closes the menu, and the same keys then chose the wrong option. ADR
  0071 lifts the refusal on a shown Chrome only, with the menu witnessed
  by the window server before every key. The build is this item, and it
  closes on ADR 0071's test.

  **Done (iteration 434).** `chrome_choose` takes ADR 0071's route on a
  shown Chrome on macOS and keeps `Unacted::Closed` headless and
  elsewhere; `chrome_menu` posts each key through one `osascript` call
  that reads the window server and the pointer first. The arrows are
  counted over the menu's items (`walk`): each option's own computed
  `display` read over Chrome's CSS domain, `disabled` and `selected` from
  its tree, the highlight starting at the chosen item or, with none,
  nowhere. Two guards were measured into it and written into ADR 0071's
  amendment: the menu is witnessed by **its window's number** — a key
  that reached the list after Finder came in front opened the menu again
  as another window, and the first build walked on in it and chose
  *Number 38* — and **no key is posted while the pointer is over the
  menu**, which moves its highlight (three Downs meant for *Dates* chose
  *Elderberries*). A refusal is `Unacted::Unwalked`, `NotCarriedOut` on
  the socket, and closes any menu left open with Escape. The new
  `a_closed_list_chosen_through_a_shown_chrome.rs`, against a shown
  Chrome: *Elderberries* two down past a disabled, a `hidden` option and
  a disabled group; *Dates* one up; *Honeydew* past an undisplayed option,
  with *Ice* after it so a count over the undisplayed one would not stop
  at the end; each heard as one `input` and one `change` for the option
  asked; *Honeydew* again posts nothing; *Grapes*, undisplayed, refused
  `NoItem`; a list holding nothing walked from nowhere; Finder brought in
  front mid-walk on a list of forty-five items answered `Gone`, the page hearing
  nothing; and the pointer moved into the menu mid-walk answered
  `UnderPointer`, the page hearing nothing and the menu closed. 8 of 8 with
  660's file, three runs. Mutations — the display ignored, any new menu
  taken for the witnessed one, the walk from nowhere off by one, a
  headless Chrome walked, the pointer not read — each fail a test. A
  fresh install's permission to post events is not measured: 692.

- [x] **692. Whether a fresh install may post the keys a closed list's
  menu is chosen in with, and what it answers when it may not.** *Cut

- [x] **671. A window smaller than was asked for is not a reason to refuse to
  run.** `alo --chrome` asks Chrome for a page area and stops with an error
  when it is given less: on 2026-10-26 at 02:45 Chrome's window held the page
  at **1200×571** where 1200×800 was asked, so the program never reached the
  line that says where an agent can reach it, and
  `a_file_named_is_opened_in_chrome_at_its_address` failed and stopped the
  loop. The same test passes on the same checkout minutes later, because what
  changed was the screen, not the code: that night the session was **locked**,
  and a window server with nothing on show does not offer the same usable
  area as one a person is looking at.
  **A window manager is allowed to give less than it is asked.** A smaller
  page area is a fact to report and lay the page out at, as item 643 already
  says for a window a person moves; refusing to run makes the browser's own
  startup depend on how much screen there happens to be, which is also what
  will happen on a laptop, under Stage Manager, or beside a dock. *Depends on
  nothing. Closes when:* a page area smaller than asked is said plainly on the
  terminal and used, the agent socket is still opened and answered, and a test
  fixes the available area small enough to force it rather than waiting for a
  screen to misbehave.

  window was given whenever it holds a page of a whole size, and refuses
  (`NotFitted`) only a window holding a page of no size; `Placed::unlike`
  says how the page differs from what was asked, and `alo --chrome` prints
  it — *"Chrome's window was given less room than the 1200×800 CSS pixels
  asked, and the page is laid out at the 1200×571 it holds"* — and runs on,

- [ ] **676. ★ A read that is answered when the page has settled.** *ADR 0002's
  surface. **needs ADR**.* `docs/contracts/agent-socket.md` says plainly that
  version 1 does not **watch**: *"There is no subscription. A caller asks and
  is answered."* That is the right rule and this item does not break it — but
  the consequence today is that an agent which has just acted **cannot tell
  when the page has finished reacting.** It sleeps a guessed number of
  milliseconds and reads again, which is exactly the guessing this browser
  exists to refuse, moved one level up. An agent that fills a field, waits
  200 ms and reads a tree the page is still rebuilding has read a lie, and
  nothing in the protocol told it so.
  The shape that keeps ADR 0002: **still one ask, still one answer** —
  `{"v":1,"ask":"read","tab":ADDRESS,"when":"settled"}`. The browser answers
  when the page has stopped changing, and if it never does, it refuses by
  kind (`NotSettled`, with how long it waited) rather than answering a tree
  it does not trust. No subscription, no stream, no callback: the caller is
  still asking a question and getting one answer to it.
  What "settled" means has to be **decided, not guessed**, which is why this
  needs an ADR. Chrome offers real signals — `Page.lifecycleEvent` with
  `networkIdle` and `networkAlmostIdle`, `Page.frameStoppedLoading` — and our
  own engine has its own task queue and knows when it is empty. The two must
  mean the same thing to an agent or the answer depends on the renderer, which
  ADR 0058 § 6 forbids in substance even where it allows it in rendering.
  *Depends on 630. Closes when:* the ADR is accepted; `read … "when":"settled"`
  is answered after the page is quiet on both renderers, asserted against a
  page that keeps working for a known time; a page that never settles is
  refused by kind with the wait in it; and `when` absent behaves exactly as
  version 1 does today, so no caller changes.
  ***Decided (2026-10-26): ADR 0065.*** Not watching: the tree is exposed once,
  when asked, to a caller the grants allow; only *when* within a bounded wait
  changes. **Settled** is decided on this process's own records, so it means
  the same through Chrome and on the engine: nothing of the page's owed (from
  the holds ADR 0060 keeps, or the renderer's own report of what it owes) and
  the tree identical in two reads 500 ms apart. Chrome's `networkIdle` may wake
  it sooner and never decides. Not settled in 10 s is refused as `NotSettled`,
  saying whether the page was still owed or still changing, with no tree. Quiet
  and ceiling are not the caller's in this version.

- [ ] **677. ★ A verb says what it changed.** An agent that acts must re-read
  the whole tree to learn what its own action did, compare two trees itself,
  and hope nothing else moved meanwhile. The browser already knows: it decided
  the verb, carried it into the document, and drew the page again (`renderer.rs`
  — *decide, change, draw again*). What it knows it does not say.
  An `act` answer gains `changed`: the nodes whose name, states or text differ
  from the tree the verb was decided against, each by `node` and what differs.
  **Not a tree, and not a stream** — the boxes that are not the same any more,
  which is the smallest true answer to *what did I just do*. A verb that
  changed nothing says `"changed":[]`, which is itself worth knowing: a click
  that moved nothing is a click that probably missed its meaning.
  This is also the honest answer to item 500, which says a box's id is good
  only for the tree it was read from: if the browser says which ids moved, an
  agent does not have to discover it by diffing.
  *Depends on 630. Closes when:* `put_text` reports the field's own box and
  nothing else; a verb that makes a page add or remove boxes reports those;
  a verb that changes nothing reports an empty list; and the same order driven
  through both renderers reports the same changes, differing only as item 630
  says the two trees may.

- [ ] **678. The record can be read back by the person it was kept for.**
  `agent_record.rs` writes what an agent read and changed, on whose approval,
  with a cause on every request — and **nothing reads it out.** A record a
  person cannot read is a promise made to an auditor who does not exist. The
  designer's state 06 (*"What happened, and what did not"*) is a view of
  exactly this, so the data has to be askable before that screen can be built.
  `{"v":1,"ask":"record"}` over the socket, and the same for the window to
  draw: what was read, what was changed, what was refused, under whose grant,
  in order, with the renderer each was done through.
  *Depends on 634. Closes when:* a run that fills a form and is refused once
  answers a record naming both, the refusal included — **a record that only
  lists what succeeded is a record of nothing** — and the window can be given
  the same without reaching into the browser process's memory.

  application inside the application, its program where a Chromium build
  puts it (`bundle::CHROMIUM`, `Bundle::chromium`); 720 puts alo's own

  redrawn by another renderer; its failure is said. What draws a page is

  driven by this browser* on the terminal and in the frame, and to an agent

## K. ★ The agent, on somebody else's pages

The reason this exists rather than a faster fork. ADR 0002 holds here or it does
not, and this is where it is found out.

- [x] **131. The agent reads and acts on ordinary web pages** through the same
  tree — no screenshot, no scraping, no coordinates.
  *Depends on 68, 81. Closes when:* a frozen real page is read and driven by
  name, with the same verbs and the same refusals.
  ***Done (iteration 295).*** `web-a-form`, httpbin's copy of the HTML
  specification's pizza form, is read and filled by the words on it. Its
  three fields are filled, then its textarea, then a size and two
  toppings, and every one is read back. `web-first-website`'s links are
  followed by their words, to the URL resolved against where it was served.
  Ambiguous, NotOperable, NotAField and NotFound refuse there as on alo's
  screens. The form found three things alo's own pages never had:
  - A field's text inside its wrapping `<label>` was dropped from the tree,
    so an agent could not read back what it put in.
  - `PutText` into a `<textarea>` was reported done and wrote a `value`
    attribute that nothing draws or reads. Its content holds it now, until
    469.
  - `PutText` into a `time` field was accepted and drawn by nothing. It is
    refused by name now (`Refusal::Unbuilt`), until 388.
  Tests: `alo-corpus`' `an_agent_on_somebody_elses_page.rs`, with a
  reference render of the filled form (`cases/web-a-form/filled.png`), and
  `alo-agent`'s `a_field_on_somebody_elses_form.rs`. Submitting the form is
  468's.
  ***Next, by the owner's choice (2026-10-12).*** Both dependencies are done and
  nothing blocks it. It is taken before the remaining shell work because it is
  the item this project justifies itself by: if ADR 0002 does not hold on
  somebody else's page, that is worth finding out now and not after another
  month of CSS. The owner's standing goal is a browser a person installs,
  searches with, and drives by agent; of those three this is the only part
  already unblocked, and 477 to 479 record that the first is stage 4 work no
  loop may open.

- [ ] **132. Across frames**, without becoming a way around the same-origin
  policy. *Depends on 86, 131. Needs ADR* — this is a security boundary an agent
  could be used to cross.

- [ ] **133. Under grants, and recorded**: what it read, what it did, on whose
  approval — `alo-os` ADR 0001's model reaching the web.
  *Depends on 67, 93, 131.*

- [ ] **134. Agent-driven navigation, and a page that changes underneath an
  agent mid-action.** The failure ADR 0003 was written for, on a page nobody

**Exit gate** (`ROADMAP.md`): a person uses it as their browser for a week and
reaches for another one only for a site they can name. An agent completes a real
task on a site nobody wrote for us, and the record afterwards says what it read
and what it changed.

# Queue — stage 3

`ROADMAP.md`: **the legacy tail.** *"Deliberately last, and possibly never
finished — a choice, not a failure. Refusing this list is what made stages 1 and
2 survivable."*

**Nothing here is taken because it is next.** Every item below is opened by a
**page in the corpus that fails because of it**, and by nothing else — not by a
specification listing a feature, not by a queue position, and not by a loop
looking for something to do. `ROADMAP.md` says it plainly: *let a broken render
schedule the work.* `LOOP.md`'s stage-boundary rules say what that means for an
iteration.

So every item here is written `blocked: no page yet`, and stays that way until
somebody adds the page. That is not a placeholder — it is the state the item is
actually in, and a loop that started one anyway would be building stage 3 for
its own sake, which is the thing this stage exists to refuse.

- [ ] **135. Quirks mode.** `alo-dom` already records the doctype signal and
  refuses to honour it (law 1). This is where a page that needs it gets it.
  *blocked: no page yet. Needs ADR* — law 1 refuses quirks mode outright, so
  implementing it is a change to the constitution rather than an item.

- [ ] **136. Floats as layout, and CSS table layout.** The two that most often
  turn an old page into a column of rubble.
  *blocked: no page yet. Cut before starting*; they are two items and probably
  more.

- [ ] **137. `document.write`, live `HTMLCollection`s, and the DOM as it was
  before it was a specification.** *blocked: no page yet. Depends on 80.*

- [ ] **138. Legacy character encodings, and detecting them.** The tables are
  already rented (queue item 51 brought `encoding_rs` for the declared ones);
  what is owed is **detection** — guessing from the shape of the bytes when
  nobody has said. This engine does not guess today, and that is stated in
  `alo-net::encoding`.
  *blocked: no page yet.*

- [ ] **139. XML, XHTML and XSLT.** *blocked: no page yet. Cut before
  starting.*

- [ ] **140. `frameset`.** *blocked: no page yet. Depends on 86.*

- [ ] **141. Vendor prefixes, and anything that exists only for a page written
  before 2015.** *blocked: no page yet.*

- [ ] **142. The sloppy-mode corners of JavaScript that only old code reaches.**
  Among them Annex B's `var` of the same name as a `catch` parameter
  (`catch (e) { var e; }`), which item 210 refuses as not a program.
  *blocked: no page yet. Depends on 72.*

**There is no exit gate**, and that is the design. Stage 3 is a standing offer
rather than a milestone: it is finished when nobody is finding broken pages any
more, which is not a state anybody declares.

# Queue — stage 4

`ROADMAP.md`: **a browser somebody chooses.** Product work, and **gated:
nothing here starts until stage 2's exit gate is met.**

**A loop cannot open this stage.** Stage 2's gate is *"a person uses it as their
browser for a week and reaches for another one only for a site they can name"* —
which is a judgement a person makes and a loop must never make on their behalf.
When stage 2's queue empties, the loop writes `LOOP COMPLETE` and stops; a

**Exit gate** (`ROADMAP.md`): somebody outside alo chooses this browser, on a
machine we did not set up, and stays.

---

## After stage 4

Nothing. `ROADMAP.md` names four stages and this queue now covers all of them,
which means **the loop can always say what is next** — and, at the two places
where only a person can decide, can say that instead.

## Never in this queue

- **Legacy compatibility, before stage 3.** Quirks mode, floats-as-layout,
  CSS-table layout, the old DOM surface. Refusing these is what makes the scope
  survivable, and stage 3 takes them only when a real page forces one.
- **`unsafe`**, without an ADR.
- **Anything measured against a conformance percentage** rather than against alo
  and then against real pages that fail.
- **Anything in `ROADMAP.md`'s "Not built, and not by accident"**: DRM and EME,
  proprietary codecs, telemetry of any kind, a search deal, and our own shaper,
  codec or TLS stack. A later stage adopting one of these quietly is exactly
  what that section exists to prevent.

*(The JavaScript engine used to be on this list, with "stage 2, and only when a
page we need requires it" beside it. Stage 2 is here, so it is item 69.)*
